title: Claude Certified Architect — Professional
disclaimer: Practice questions authored from the official exam guide. These are NOT official exam items.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder describes a business problem and the outcome the business wants. Which Domain 1 objective is the architect carrying out when turning that description into a Claude-based AI solution?

options.text: Selecting the appropriate architectural pattern for the use case
Translating the business problem into a Claude-based AI solution
Aligning the completed solution to the business value pillars

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the objective itself plus its two closest neighbours in the same domain (1.3 pattern selection and 1.6 value alignment), which is exactly the confusion the mapping item is meant to expose. A fourth option would add filler rather than a new distinction.

distractorRationale.a: Probes whether the learner skips the translation step and jumps straight to choosing a pattern, which is objective 1.3.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion with objective 1.6, which applies to a solution that already exists rather than producing the first one.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.1 is named as translating business problems into Claude-based AI solutions. Pattern selection (1.3) and business value alignment (1.6) both presuppose that a Claude-based solution has already been defined.

whyWrong.a: Choosing among workflow, agentic and augmented LLM is objective 1.3, and it runs after the solution has been translated.
whyWrong.c: Mapping a solution to efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs is objective 1.6, a later alignment step.

explanation.analogy: Translation comes before architecture: the problem statement is the brief, the pattern is the drawing style, and the value pillars are what the client signs off on.
explanation.takeaway: 1.1 turns a business problem into a Claude-based AI solution; everything else in Domain 1 follows that step.
explanation.deepDive: The Domain 1 objective list is a sequence of distinct activities: translate (1.1), design the end-to-end flow (1.2), select a pattern (1.3), design multi-agent systems (1.4), decompose (1.5), align to value (1.6).

questions.prompt: Objective 1.2 describes an end-to-end architecture as a four-stage flow. Which sequence matches it?

options.text: input → processing → output → feedback loops
output → input → processing → feedback loops
input → feedback loops → processing → output

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the guide's sequence plus two reorderings that reuse exactly the same four stage names, so the learner must recall the order rather than recognise the vocabulary.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that output re-enters as input, collapsing the distinct feedback loop stage into the first one.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reading the flow as linear rather than cyclical, which removes the feedback loop stage from its closing position.

explanation.correct: The guide names the flow as input → processing → output → feedback loops. Inputs arrive first, are processed, produce an output, and the feedback loops close the cycle.

whyWrong.a: Feedback loops are a stage of their own in the objective; they are not the same thing as the input stage.
whyWrong.c: The objective places feedback loops last, after output, not second. This ordering turns a loop into a one-way pipeline.

explanation.analogy: It is a four-beat cycle: take the request, do the work, hand back the answer, and use what came back to improve the next pass.
explanation.takeaway: Memorise the Domain 1 flow as input → processing → output → feedback loops.
explanation.deepDive: The feedback stage is what makes the architecture end-to-end rather than a single call: without it the design stops at the moment an output is produced.

source.section: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)

questions.prompt: Objective 1.2 asks the architect to design an end-to-end architecture. What does that word require the design to cover?

options.text: Every stage the objective names, not only the part that produces an answer
Only the model call that produces the output, since that is where the work happens
Just the intake and the final reply, leaving the intermediate steps to implementation
The feedback loops alone, as a stage that is easily left out

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because 'end-to-end' invites three distinct narrowings, each a real way a design gets truncated: the single model call, the two end points, and one named stage on its own. Three options would have had to merge two of those readings into a single distractor and lose which one the learner had in mind.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating the whole architecture as its one model call, which is one common truncation of the flow.
distractorRationale.b: Probes keeping the visible end points and treating input, processing and output as plumbing rather than design.
distractorRationale.d: Probes singling out the feedback stage as the interesting part and demoting the rest of the flow to background.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.2 asks for an end-to-end architecture, so the design has to cover the whole chain the objective names rather than the part of it that happens to be interesting.

whyWrong.a: The model call is the processing stage, one of four. A design that stops there omits the output and feedback stages the objective names after it.
whyWrong.b: Input, processing, output and feedback loops are all enumerated in the objective. Treating the middle as implementation detail leaves two named stages outside the design.
whyWrong.d: Selecting one stage is the opposite of end-to-end. Feedback loops sit at the end of the same chain as input, processing and output, not instead of them.

explanation.takeaway: End-to-end covers all four stages the objective names, and the feedback loops are one a design can easily leave out.
explanation.deepDive: Read the parenthetical as the definition: the arrow chain is what 'end-to-end' is standing for. An architecture that stops at the output has designed one stage of the four, which is a gap worth looking for in a design review.

source.section: 1.2 Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which patterns does objective 1.3 name for CCAR-P architecture selection?

options.text: workflow
retrieval-augmented generation
agentic
augmented LLM

questions.optionCountRationale: The objective enumerates exactly three patterns, so a select-all item is the honest format. A fourth option is needed as the one real technique a learner might wrongly import from elsewhere, which is the misconception worth probing.

distractorRationale.b: Probes answering with a real and important LLM technique that this objective does not enumerate. The learner must recall the exact list rather than list plausible techniques.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.3 names three patterns: workflow, agentic, and augmented LLM. That enumeration is the whole content of the objective as written.

whyWrong.b: Retrieval-augmented generation is not among the three patterns named in objective 1.3, whatever its merits elsewhere in the guide.

explanation.takeaway: The 1.3 pattern set is exactly three names: workflow, agentic, augmented LLM.
explanation.deepDive: Because the objective gives no criteria for choosing among them, the safest exam posture is to be able to recite the set precisely and to resist substituting techniques you know are real but are not listed here.

source.section: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)

questions.prompt: A reviewer claims the agentic pattern in objective 1.3 already covers the multi-agent work listed under objective 1.4. Which reply matches the guide?

options.text: Correct; agentic and multi-agent are one objective under two names
Correct; 1.4 only repeats the agentic pattern with fresher wording
No; 1.3 enumerates patterns, and 1.4 separately covers multi-agent systems

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the boundary-preserving answer plus the two ways learners collapse adjacent objectives. Both errors are restatements of the same merge, but they differ enough that merging them would weaken the diagnostic value.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating closely worded adjacent objectives as synonyms, a real risk in a domain list this terse.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the subtler version: accepting the merge while assuming the second objective is simply restated for emphasis.

explanation.correct: The guide lists 1.3 and 1.4 as separate objectives, each with its own verb and its own object. Close wording is not the same objective twice, so a reviewer's claim that one covers the other does not hold.

whyWrong.a: Two distinct numbered objectives are not one objective renamed, and each names a different design activity.
whyWrong.c: 1.4 adds orchestration strategies, which the 1.3 pattern enumeration does not mention.

explanation.takeaway: Pattern selection (1.3) and multi-agent design (1.4) are separate objectives, not two names for the same work.
explanation.deepDive: Keeping them apart matters when you read an item: if the question is about choosing between named patterns, it is 1.3; if it is about coordinating several agents, it is 1.4.

source.section: 1.3 Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)

questions.prompt: Objective 1.4 asks the architect to design multi-agent systems and one further thing. Which?

options.text: Business value pillars such as cost and performance SLAs
Orchestration strategies for those agents
Decomposition techniques for complex problem solving

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the phrase the objective actually carries, plus the two adjacent Domain 1 activities a learner is most likely to splice into it. Both distractors are real domain topics, which is what makes them useful rather than filler.

distractorRationale.a: Probes importing objective 1.6 into a design activity, which is a common over-reach when a business case is being written.
distractorRationale.c: Probes importing objective 1.5, since breaking work into agent-sized parts looks like decomposition.

explanation.correct: The objective reads: design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies. Orchestration is the second half of the wording, and it is the part most often dropped.

whyWrong.a: Value pillars belong to objective 1.6 and describe what the solution delivers, not how agents are coordinated.
whyWrong.c: Decomposition is objective 1.5. Splitting work is not the same activity as deciding how agents coordinate once they exist.

explanation.takeaway: 1.4 is two-part: multi-agent systems plus orchestration strategies.
explanation.deepDive: Orchestration is what makes multi-agent design an architecture decision rather than a list of agents. If an item mentions coordination between agents, it is pointing at 1.4.

source.section: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies

questions.prompt: Several agents must divide a research task between them. What does objective 1.4 expect the architect to bring to that problem?

options.text: Whatever coordination behaviour the underlying model happens to provide
A deliberate orchestration strategy designed for how the agents work
A standardisation on one pattern for the whole system, applied without further design
Nothing; multi-agent designs simply run each agent on its own

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the objective's design responsibility, plus three positions that would remove or relocate it — inheriting default behaviour, standardising on a single pattern for the whole system, or running the agents with no coordination at all. The standardisation option earns its place because it is a defensible architecture in its own right and is the one a learner reaches for instead of answering 1.4.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating orchestration as something inherited from the model rather than designed, which would make the objective trivial.
distractorRationale.c: Probes assuming that 'multi-agent' means agents run independently, removing the coordination decision the objective is built around.
distractorRationale.d: Probes routing a multi-agent design question to 1.3's pattern selection. Choosing one pattern for the whole system answers 1.3, but the prompt has already committed to several agents, so the open question is 1.4's.

explanation.correct: Naming orchestration strategies as part of the objective implies the architect chooses how agents coordinate. That implication is drawn from the wording; objective 1.4 does not enumerate any specific strategies, so the answer stays at the level of the design decision itself.

whyWrong.a: If coordination were inherited by default there would be nothing to design, and the objective would not need to name orchestration strategies.
whyWrong.c: Independent agents with no coordination are not what a multi-agent system means here; the strategy is how they work together.
whyWrong.d: Standardising on a single pattern is a legitimate answer to 1.3, but it settles the pattern question rather than the coordination question. Here the agents already exist and the scenario is how they divide the work, which is what orchestration strategies address.

explanation.takeaway: Objective 1.4 is a design decision about how agents coordinate, even though the guide lists no named strategies.
explanation.deepDive: Orchestration is the second half of objective 1.4's wording, and it is the half that makes multi-agent design an architectural decision: how the agents coordinate is chosen and designed, not inherited from whatever arrangement presents itself.

source.section: 1.4 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies

questions.reviewNote: Objective 1.4 names orchestration strategies without enumerating any, so no specific strategy can be checked against the guide. The keyed option stays at the level of the design decision the wording implies; it does not name or require any particular coordination pattern.

questions.prompt: Objective 1.5 calls for decomposition of a complex problem. What exactly is being decomposed?

options.text: The complex problem itself, into parts that can each be worked on
The end-to-end architecture into its input, processing, output and feedback stages
The candidate architectural patterns into their individual components

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options cover the problem level and the two design levels that decomposition is most often confused with, 1.2's stages and 1.3's patterns. All three are similarly long so neither size nor order signals the answer.

distractorRationale.a: Probes transferring the word 'decomposition' onto the architecture flow from objective 1.2, where the stages are already given.
distractorRationale.c: Probes transferring it onto pattern selection, where the three named patterns are already a fixed enumeration.

explanation.correct: The object of decomposition is the complex problem. The parts it yields are what makes the problem solvable step by step.

whyWrong.a: The architecture stages are already enumerated by the guide in 1.2; they are not something the architect is breaking up.
whyWrong.c: The patterns are already enumerated in 1.3. Decomposing them is not an activity the guide asks for anywhere in Domain 1.

explanation.takeaway: In 1.5 you decompose the problem, never the architecture or the pattern list.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 1.2 gives you the stages and 1.3 gives you the pattern names as fixed content. 1.5 is the only Domain 1 objective whose output is not one of those given structures but a set of problem parts.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which of these are business value pillars named in objective 1.6?

options.text: Cost
Performance SLAs
Efficiency
Accuracy

questions.optionCountRationale: The objective names five pillars, so a select-all item is the honest way to test recall of the list. The single wrong option is a real and important quality that the guide raises in other domains but does not include here.

distractorRationale.b: Probes importing a real quality attribute from elsewhere in the guide and treating it as part of the business value pillar list.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.6 names efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs. Efficiency, cost and performance SLAs are three of those five.

whyWrong.b: Accuracy is not one of the pillars this objective names. It matters elsewhere in the guide, but it is not in the 1.6 list.

explanation.takeaway: The five 1.6 pillars are efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs.
explanation.deepDive: The full list matters as much as the members you are shown. Efficiency, transformation and productivity are easy to half-remember, and performance SLAs is the only pillar phrased with a commitment attached.

questions.prompt: Under CCAR-P objective 2.1, what is the basis for choosing a Claude model for a workload?

options.text: Weigh the trade-offs between Claude models and pick the one that fits the workload
Default to the most capable Claude model so no trade-off analysis is ever needed
Default to whichever model other teams already use, to stay consistent
Choose the model with the largest context window, so nothing is ever truncated

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the misconception here is a family, not one error: defaulting to the strongest model, copying someone else's pick, and treating context-window size as a proxy for fit are three distinct ways of dodging the trade-off analysis the objective names.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the 'always use the most capable model' habit, which removes the trade-off judgement 2.1 asks for.
distractorRationale.b: Probes inheriting a model choice by precedent instead of evaluating the workload.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating a single specification as a proxy for overall fit.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.1 is 'Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs'. The objective is the act of weighing trade-offs and choosing the model that fits the workload, not a rule about a specific model.

whyWrong.a: Always taking the strongest model eliminates the comparison that the objective requires; it is a decision rule about capability, not about trade-offs.
whyWrong.b: Reusing another team's model is consistency, not selection. The objective asks you to evaluate trade-offs for the workload in front of you.
whyWrong.d: Context-window size is one property. Treating it as the selector removes the other trade-offs from consideration entirely.

explanation.analogy: Model selection is load-bearing choice, not brand loyalty: you do not specify the same steel for a bookshelf and a bridge girder.
explanation.takeaway: Objective 2.1 is about weighing trade-offs per workload, not defaulting to one model for everything.
explanation.deepDive: Two trade-off questions are always live: is the most capable model actually needed for this workload, and what does the cheaper or faster alternative give up? Answering 2.1 means putting a specific workload behind both questions and naming which way the balance falls, rather than defaulting on habit.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.2 names three things to design together. Which set is it?

options.text: System prompts, reusable templates, and guardrails
Model choice, chunk size, and retrieval strategy
Retrieval sources, in-context examples, and step-by-step reasoning

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the objective's own three artefacts, plus two near-neighbour sets — one that mixes a 2.1 decision with retrieval terms, and one that restates 2.3's prompt-engineering themes in different words. Three is the honest count because the confusion worth testing is misfiling a neighbouring bullet's list, not enumerating extra artefacts.

distractorRationale.b: Mixes a 2.1 decision with retrieval terms that 2.2 never names, probing whether candidates sort objectives by topic rather than by wording.
distractorRationale.c: Restates the kinds of thing objective 2.3 is about rather than the artefacts 2.2 names, probing overlap between neighbouring objectives.

explanation.correct: The bullet reads 'Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails'. Those three are one design task: the instructions, the reusable structure they sit in, and the boundaries that keep the assistant inside it.

whyWrong.b: Model choice is 2.1's, and 2.2 names only system prompts, templates and guardrails. None of the three things in this option appears there.
whyWrong.c: In-context examples and step-by-step reasoning are prompt-engineering techniques, which belong to 2.3. Retrieval sources are not named in 2.2 either — the objective names system prompts, templates, and guardrails.

explanation.analogy: A system prompt is the job description, the template is the form it is written on, and guardrails are the limits on what the role is allowed to do.
explanation.takeaway: 2.2 is about the prompt layer: instructions, reusable templates, and guardrails, designed together.
explanation.deepDive: Because these objectives sit next to each other in the same domain, most mistakes in this area are misattributions rather than misunderstandings of the mechanics. Anchoring the exact wording of each bullet is a reliable first step.

source.section: 2.2 Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails

questions.prompt: Which three prompt-engineering techniques does objective 2.3 name explicitly?

options.text: Few-shot examples, RAG retrieval, and fine-tuning
Reusable templates, shared context files, and versioned prompts
Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, each a plausible technique list drawn from elsewhere in the guide. The objective's own parenthetical names exactly three items, so there is no honest basis for a fourth.

distractorRationale.a: Probes importing techniques the objective does not list: only few-shot appears in 2.3, so retrieval and fine-tuning are not part of it.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the reuse-versus-technique boundary inside Domain 2: packaging prompt content so it can be reused is not one of the three techniques 2.3 names.

explanation.correct: The bullet reads 'Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)'. All three named techniques are ways of shaping a single request.

whyWrong.a: Only few-shot appears alongside them. Objective 2.3 names zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought, and nothing else.
whyWrong.b: None of these three is named in 2.5, which lists caching, modular prompts and Skills. Reusable templates belong to the artefacts 2.2 names, not to 2.3's list of techniques.

explanation.analogy: 2.3 is about how you phrase the request; 2.5 is about how you ship and reuse the prompt around it.
explanation.takeaway: 2.3 names three techniques — zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought — and nothing else.
explanation.deepDive: Both 2.3 and 2.5 are single-line bullets with no supporting text, so the reliable study move is to memorise the lists verbatim and recognise the boundary: 2.3 shapes one request, 2.5 reuses prompt content across requests.

source.section: 2.3 Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

questions.prompt: A reviewer lists five Domain 2 terms: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, caching, and modular prompts. Which split matches the guide?

options.text: All five are prompt engineering techniques named under 2.3
Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought are 2.5; caching and modular prompts are 2.3
Zero-shot and few-shot are 2.2; the other three are 2.3
Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought are 2.3; caching and modular prompts are 2.5

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options covering the three errors worth making on a list-splitting question: merging the two lists, swapping them, and filing the techniques under the neighbouring artefact objective. Each distractor is a distinct misfiling, so a three-option version would have to merge two of them and lose which one the learner had in mind.

distractorRationale.a: Probes collapsing every Domain 2 term into one bucket, which is what happens when the three lists are learned as one vocabulary.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the outright swap, the error made when caching and modular prompts are remembered as techniques rather than reuse strategies.
distractorRationale.d: Probes filing the techniques under the prompt-artefact objective because 2.2 and 2.3 share the word prompt.

explanation.correct: The five terms divide cleanly between two adjacent objectives: 2.3 names the prompting techniques and 2.5 names the prompt reuse strategies. Merging them into one list, or swapping the two halves, misstates both objectives.

whyWrong.a: Objective 2.3 names three techniques and nothing else. Caching and modular prompts are named under 2.5, so merging the lists misstates both objectives.
whyWrong.b: This reverses the two. The techniques that shape a single request are 2.3's; the strategies that reuse prompt content across requests are 2.5's.
whyWrong.d: Objective 2.2 names the prompt artefacts - system prompts, templates, guardrails - and none of the five terms appears there, so the split is wrong as well as incomplete.

explanation.takeaway: Adjacent objectives split by object: the list that shapes one request is 2.3's, and the list that reuses prompt content across requests is 2.5's.
explanation.deepDive: The split that does the work is object-based: 2.3 is about shaping a request, 2.5 is about reusing prompt content. Because neither bullet explains itself, the lists are the reliable thing to learn.

questions.prompt: A team must decide what to keep in each request's context window. Which objective owns that decision?

options.text: 2.5 — Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
2.4 — Optimize context windows and manage token usage
2.1 — Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options quoting the neighbouring Domain 2 objectives. Deciding what belongs in the window is easy to misfile as token saving (2.5) or model choice (2.1), and only those two misfilings are worth testing.

distractorRationale.a: Probes conflating reducing what you send with reusing what you already send — both are called 'token efficiency'.
distractorRationale.b: Probes assuming any cost-shaped decision is really a model-selection decision.

explanation.correct: 2.4 is literally 'Optimize context windows and manage token usage'. Choosing what goes into the window and how many tokens that costs is the decision this objective owns.

whyWrong.a: 2.5 is about reuse: its strategies change how often the same prompt content is reused, not what a given request carries.
whyWrong.b: 2.1 decides which model to use. That choice may interact with context cost, but it is a different decision from what belongs in the window.

explanation.analogy: 2.4 decides what to pack for the trip; 2.5 decides what you can leave at home because it is already on the shelf.
explanation.takeaway: Context contents and token volume are 2.4; prompt reuse across requests is 2.5.
explanation.deepDive: Objectives 2.4 and 2.5 are the pair most often confused in this domain because both reduce token cost. The test that separates them: are you changing one request's contents (2.4), or changing how the same prompt content is reused across requests (2.5)?

source.section: 2.4 Optimize context windows and manage token usage

questions.prompt: Which three strategies does objective 2.5 name for reusing prompt content?

options.text: Chunking, indexing, and retrieval tuning
Few-shot, zero-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting
Caching, modular prompts, and Skills

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the reuse strategies 2.5 names, the technique list 2.3 names, and a retrieval-shaped list that 2.5 does not name. The objective's parenthetical fixes the count at three, so a fourth option would have to be invented.

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling retrieval-shaped concepts into a reuse objective; none of the three is among the strategies 2.5 names.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing how one request is phrased with how prompt content is reused across many requests.

explanation.correct: The bullet reads 'Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)'. All three are about not rebuilding the same prompt content every time.

whyWrong.a: Chunking, indexing, and retrieval tuning are not named in 2.5's reuse list. They are neither the content being reused nor a way of packaging it.
whyWrong.c: That is 2.3's list. Those techniques change the content of one request; 2.5 is about reusing prompt content across requests.

explanation.analogy: Reuse strategies are stationery and templates on a shared desk; prompting techniques are what you write on the page in front of you.
explanation.takeaway: 2.5's three named reuse strategies are caching, modular prompts, and Skills.
explanation.deepDive: The objective's verb is implement, and all three named strategies act on prompt content that would otherwise be rebuilt on every request. That shared object is what separates them from the techniques in 2.3, which change the content of a single request instead.

source.section: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)

questions.prompt: An extraction service resends the same 6,000-token instruction block on every request, followed by a short varying input. Which change addresses the repeated content itself?

options.text: Trim the instruction block down to its opening 500 tokens on every request
Switch to the smallest available model, whatever the extraction task needs
Move the instruction block into a few-shot example so it reads as data
Turn on prompt caching for the repeated block so its content is reused across requests

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because all three distractors are realistic optimisations a team would actually try: truncating, relocating, and downsizing. Each fails for a different reason, which is the point of the item.

distractorRationale.b: Probes treating deletion as optimisation, discarding instructions the model needs to extract correctly.
distractorRationale.c: Probes believing that re-labelling static content as an example changes how often it has to be sent.
distractorRationale.d: Probes swapping a prompt problem for a model change, which risks quality and still resends the same tokens.

explanation.correct: Caching is the reuse strategy objective 2.5 names for prompt content that would otherwise be rebuilt or resent on every request, and the repeated block in this scenario is exactly that content.

whyWrong.b: Truncating throws away instructions the extraction depends on. The saving comes from the system no longer doing the work properly.
whyWrong.c: Re-framing the block as an example changes what the model treats as instruction versus data; it does not change the fact that the same content is sent on every request.
whyWrong.d: The problem is repeated static content, not model capability. A smaller model still receives the same repeated block, and quality may drop.

explanation.analogy: Printing the same 6,000-token manual on every job order: the fix is to stop reprinting it, not to shorten the manual.
explanation.takeaway: 2.5 names caching as the strategy for reusing prompt content across requests, and the repeated block is the content it is for.
explanation.deepDive: Caching is the strategy that fits a scenario built around the same block of prompt content being resent unchanged every time: the repetition is the thing being reused, so the fix belongs to the reuse objective rather than to a rewrite of the instructions.

source.section: 2.5 Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)

questions.reviewNote: Objective 2.5 names caching as a single word and defines none of the three strategies. The keyed option depends on prompt-caching mechanics — stable-prefix ordering and prefix reuse — that the guide does not state, and the cost and time-to-first-token effects are likewise unstated. Needs a fuller guide section or official Anthropic documentation before it can be presented as exam-aligned.

questions.prompt: Which 2.5 strategy keeps shared sections in one maintained place and composes them into many prompts?

options.text: Prompt caching, which reuses prompt content that would otherwise be resent each time
Modular prompts, where shared sections are separate reusable modules
Zero-shot prompting, which supplies the task with no examples

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the reuse strategy named for composable structure, the other reuse strategy 2.5 names beside it, and a technique from 2.3 that shares the word 'prompt' but nothing else.

distractorRationale.b: Probes conflating the two reuse strategies named in the same objective: caching is not described in terms of composable structure.
distractorRationale.c: Probes grabbing the most familiar prompting term when the question is about reuse.

explanation.correct: Modular prompts are the structural strategy: shared sections become separate modules that are composed into whichever prompts need them, so the shared content is maintained in one place.

whyWrong.b: Caching and modular prompts are two separate strategies named side by side under the same objective. Keeping shared sections in one maintained place and composing them into many prompts is what 'modular' describes; caching is the strategy for reusing content that would otherwise be resent.
whyWrong.c: Zero-shot is a technique from 2.3 about including no examples. It says nothing about how a prompt is structured or reused.

explanation.analogy: Modular prompts are shared header and footer components assembled per document; caching is keeping the same already-printed cover on the shelf.
explanation.takeaway: Modular prompts are named for composing shared sections into many prompts; caching is a separate strategy the objective does not define.
explanation.deepDive: Modular prompts and caching are named side by side under 2.5, so telling them apart is a matter of what each name describes: one keeps shared sections in a maintained place for composition into many prompts, the other reuses content that would otherwise be sent again.

The answer rests on the standard sense of 'modular' — shared sections kept in one place and composed into many prompts — and rejecting caching depends on a modular-versus-caching distinction the objective does not draw. questions.prompt: A CI/CD agent can read build logs, rerun a failed job, deploy to production, and rotate signing keys. The team only ever needs to read logs and rerun jobs. Which finding does objective 3.1 ask you to record?

options.text: The agent's tool calls are not traced in enough detail to explain a bad run
The deploy tool can be invoked by any caller that reaches the subnet
The model in use is slower than the accuracy this job actually requires
The agent holds deploy and key-rotation capability that its role does not require

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the finding 3.1 is about, plus three that are real but belong to 3.4, 3.2 and 3.3 respectively. Three of the four are genuine problems a reviewer could raise about this configuration, so the item tests attribution rather than whether the learner can invent a finding.

distractorRationale.b: Probes misfiling a traceability complaint under capability evaluation. Selecting monitoring strategies is 3.4.
distractorRationale.c: Probes misfiling an access-control complaint under capability evaluation. Analysing authentication and authorization is 3.2.
distractorRationale.d: Probes misfiling an accuracy-latency complaint under capability evaluation. The objective 3.1 names is about tool and agent configuration, not model performance.

explanation.correct: Objective 3.1 asks you to evaluate the tool/agent configuration for capability bloat. Compared against the role, deploy and key rotation are capability the role does not require, so that is the finding the objective is about. The objective names no specific remedy, so recording the finding is what it asks for.

whyWrong.b: How well the agent's runs can be traced is a monitoring question. Analysing observability challenges and selecting monitoring strategies at scale is 3.4.
whyWrong.c: Who is allowed to invoke a tool is an access-control question. Analysing authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps is 3.2, and it holds even when the capability itself is justified.
whyWrong.d: Speed against accuracy is the trade-off objective 3.3 names. Nothing in the scenario says the model is too slow, and model performance is not what 'tool/agent configuration' refers to.

explanation.analogy: An over-broad keyring is recognised by comparing every key on it against the doors the job actually requires — that comparison is the evaluation, not a claim about which lock to change.
explanation.takeaway: 3.1 asks you to evaluate a tool or agent configuration against the role it serves.
explanation.deepDive: The evaluation is a comparison, not a verdict: list what the configuration carries, list what the role is assigned, and the gap between the two lists is the finding.

questions.reviewNote: Objective 3.1 names 'capability bloat' but never defines it. The keyed option rests on an inference - capability the role does not require is the bloat - rather than on a definition the guide states. It deliberately makes no claim about the remedy: the objective names no fix, and the previous version of this item required removal as the only defensible response. Confirm against fuller source material before treating this framing as exam-aligned.

questions.prompt: Which question belongs to objective 3.1 rather than to a neighbouring Domain 3 objective?

options.text: Which tools belong in this agent's configuration, and which does the role need?
Does this integration authenticate its callers and restrict what they may do?
Should this agent receive its context all at once or discover it progressively?

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one each from 3.1, 3.2 and 3.8. Attribution between neighbouring Domain 3 objectives is the confusion this domain most rewards testing, and the objective is phrased around the thing being evaluated — tool/agent configuration — rather than around any definition of capability bloat, which is what makes it safe to ask.

distractorRationale.b: Probes conflating configuration scope with access control. Both are things you can tighten about a risky integration, but only one of them is 3.1.
distractorRationale.c: Probes conflating which tools the agent has with how much context about them it receives. The tool set is unchanged either way.

explanation.correct: 3.1 is 'Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat'. It is concerned with what a tool or agent configuration contains, which is what deciding which tools belong in it asks.

whyWrong.b: Analysing authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps is 3.2. It asks who may invoke the tool, not whether the tool belongs there.
whyWrong.c: Evaluating progressive discovery against a monolithic context strategy is 3.8. It asks how much context arrives up front, which is a different question from which tools are configured.

explanation.analogy: 3.1 audits what is in the toolbox; 3.2 audits who is allowed to open it; 3.8 decides whether the manual is handed over whole or fetched by chapter.
explanation.takeaway: 3.1 is about what the tool or agent configuration contains, not about access control or context supply.
explanation.deepDive: The objective's subject is the configuration itself: what the tool or agent is given access to. A review starts by listing what the configuration carries and comparing that list against the work the role is actually assigned.

questions.prompt: An internal refund endpoint performs no authentication or authorization of its own. What should the architect flag under objective 3.2?

options.text: The endpoint declares no error schema, so clients cannot parse failures
The endpoint has no versioned contract, so future changes will break callers
The endpoint implements neither of the two requirements the objective names

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: two interface-design gaps that are real but out of scope, and the authentication/authorization gap the objective actually asks you to find. A fourth would be another interface concern, adding no coverage.

distractorRationale.a: Probes mistaking error-contract design for a security finding. Structured errors are an interface concern, not an authentication or authorization gap.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing interface stability with access control, which are frequently discussed in the same design reviews.

explanation.correct: The endpoint performs no authentication or authorization of its own, which is exactly the kind of gap 3.2 asks you to identify. The objective asks for the two requirements to be analysed, so the finding here is the check that is missing, not a proposed fix.

whyWrong.a: An error schema affects how clients handle failures. It concerns the interface a caller sees, not either of the two requirements objective 3.2 names.
whyWrong.b: Contract versioning is about compatibility as the interface changes over time. Neither of the two requirements objective 3.2 names is about how callers adapt to a new release.

explanation.analogy: The objective names two requirements. The finding here is that neither has been implemented at all, which is a different conversation from how one of them is handled.
explanation.takeaway: An endpoint that performs no authentication or authorization of its own is the gap objective 3.2 asks you to identify.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 3.2 is about analysing requirements to find gaps, so the exam skill is naming which of the two named requirements is unsatisfied, not proposing a fix.

source.section: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps

questions.prompt: Objective 3.2 names two requirements to analyse when looking for security gaps. A team argues that checking a password at sign-in settles the whole objective, so no further review is needed. Which reply matches the objective?

options.text: Correct; authentication and authorization are the same requirement under two names
Correct; the objective offers authentication or authorization, so meeting either one is enough
No; the objective names two requirements, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the answer that keeps the two requirements separate, plus the two distinct ways of collapsing them - reading them as one requirement under two names, and reading the objective's 'and' as a choice between alternatives. Both collapses are separable misreadings of the same clause, and a fourth would have to restate one of them.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that a pair of closely related terms names a single check. The objective lists both, so the analysis has two subjects.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reading the objective's conjunction as a choice between alternatives, which would make the second requirement optional.

explanation.correct: Objective 3.2 is 'Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps'. It names two requirements, joined by 'and'. Checking a password at sign-in discharges one of them and leaves the other unanalysed, so the gap objective 3.2 asks about is still open.

whyWrong.a: Two separately named requirements are not one requirement written twice. The objective lists both, and the analysis has to cover both.
whyWrong.c: The objective names both as requirements to analyse, not as alternatives between which a team picks. Satisfying one does not remove the other from the review.

explanation.takeaway: 3.2 names two requirements, authentication and authorization, and satisfying one is not the same as satisfying the other.
explanation.deepDive: Reading the objective's own grammar is the whole test here: it says 'authentication and authorization requirements', a conjunction, so the architect's analysis has two subjects.

source.section: 3.2 Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps

questions.prompt: A research pipeline can be built one way — slow with high accuracy — or another way — fast with lower accuracy. What makes the second option defensible under 3.3?

options.text: It is faster, so user-visible latency improves in every case
It makes fewer model calls, so it is cheaper to operate
The accuracy it gives up is acceptable for the queries this pipeline serves
It relies on defaults, so no accuracy-or-latency judgement is needed

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the three distractors fail in genuinely different ways: latency as an automatic win, a cost argument substituted for an accuracy one, and avoiding the judgement entirely. Each is a distinct way of skipping the justification.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating one side of the trade-off as self-justifying, with no reference to what accuracy is lost.
distractorRationale.c: Probes arguing cost when the objective names accuracy and latency. Cheaper is a different argument.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the 'it is just the default' dodge, which removes the justification the objective explicitly requires.

explanation.correct: The justification has to name both sides and tie them to the workload: the pipeline trades a specific amount of accuracy for latency, and that amount is acceptable for the queries it serves. That is the trade-off evaluated and the decision justified, in one sentence.

whyWrong.a: Speed is half of the trade-off, not a justification for accepting it. Nothing here establishes that lower accuracy is tolerable.
whyWrong.c: Cost is a real consideration, but this objective names accuracy and latency. Substituting a different argument does not justify this trade-off.
whyWrong.d: Defaults remove an explicit choice; they do not remove the obligation to justify why the resulting configuration fits the workload.

explanation.analogy: Skipping a summary for full text is defensible when readers only need headlines, and indefensible when they need the detail — the justification is about the reader's need.
explanation.takeaway: A configuration choice is defensible when you state what accuracy you gave up and why that is acceptable here.
explanation.deepDive: Neither side of this trade-off has a fixed number attached to it. What makes the second option defensible is the judgement that the accuracy it gives up is acceptable for this workload, and that judgement is the architect's to make.

source.section: 3.3 Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions

questions.prompt: Which question belongs to objective 3.4 rather than to a neighbouring Domain 3 objective?

options.text: Should these tools be removed from the agent's configuration?
What becomes hard to observe here, and what should be monitored at scale?
Which retrieval strategy fits this data shape and query pattern?

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one each from 3.1, 3.6, and 3.4. Attribution between neighbouring Domain 3 objectives is the confusion this domain most rewards testing.

distractorRationale.a: Probes conflating monitoring with capability scoping — both are things you can do about a risky integration.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing 'how do I see what happened' with 'how do I fetch the right thing', which are adjacent but distinct decisions.

explanation.correct: 3.4 is 'Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale'. It is concerned with what becomes invisible as a system grows and what to instrument in response.

whyWrong.a: Removing tools from an agent's configuration is capability-bloat evaluation, which is 3.1.
whyWrong.b: Matching retrieval to data shape and query pattern is 3.6. It is about what the system retrieves, not what you can see.

explanation.analogy: 3.1 asks what is in the agent's toolkit; 3.4 asks what a reviewer can see of what it did.
explanation.takeaway: 3.4 is about what becomes hard to observe as volume grows, and what to monitor because of it.
explanation.deepDive: Domain 3's objectives partition naturally into capability (3.1), security (3.2), trade-offs (3.3), visibility (3.4), retrieval (3.5, 3.6), connection mechanisms (3.7), and context strategy (3.8). Attributing a question to the right bucket is a reliable first-order study skill.

questions.prompt: Which pair of decisions does objective 3.5 put in the architect's hands?

options.text: Which Claude model to use, and what it costs per call
Which prompting technique to apply, and how many examples to include
How documents are chunked, and how they are indexed

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the RAG pipeline's own two named decisions, plus the two distractors - one model decision and one prompting decision from elsewhere in the guide. The objective names two decisions, so three options covers it without padding.

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling model economics into a pipeline-design objective, which is 2.1's territory.
distractorRationale.c: Probes treating retrieval-augmented generation as a prompting technique rather than as a pipeline with its own structure.

explanation.correct: Objective 3.5 is 'Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies'. The pipeline is built by deciding how source documents are divided and how those pieces are made findable.

whyWrong.a: Model choice and its cost sit under 2.1. They matter for a RAG system, but they are not the chunking-and-indexing decisions this objective names.
whyWrong.c: Prompting technique is 2.3. RAG is a pipeline stage with its own structural decisions, which is why the guide gives it its own objective.

explanation.analogy: Chunking is deciding how to cut a document; indexing is deciding how the shelves are labelled so the right piece can be found.
explanation.takeaway: 3.5 = building the pipeline: chunk the documents, index the pieces.
explanation.deepDive: Domain 3 splits retrieval deliberately: 3.5 covers building and indexing the store, 3.6 covers the query-time strategy. Keeping those apart resolves most retrieval questions before they start.

source.section: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies

questions.prompt: A corpus of long, consistently structured policy PDFs must be made searchable. What should drive the chunking decision?

options.text: The structure of the source documents and the questions the corpus must answer
A chunk size chosen by the number of users hitting the index
Chunking by token count, with no regard for the structure of the document

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options. The objective asks for chunking to be 'appropriate', and only three sourcing rules can honestly be offered: concurrent query load, token count in place of document structure, or the structure of the documents and the questions the corpus must answer. Inventing specific chunk sizes or overlap percentages would exceed the source.

distractorRationale.a: Probes letting an operational signal - how many users hit the index - decide a corpus-structure question.
distractorRationale.b: Probes measuring the documents in tokens while ignoring that they have a structure, which is the input 'appropriate' points back to.

explanation.correct: Objective 3.5 asks for appropriate chunking. Appropriateness comes from the material being chunked and the queries it has to serve, so structure and question type are the inputs to the decision.

whyWrong.a: Query load says nothing about how a document should be divided. The objective asks for chunking that suits the material and the questions asked of it, and concurrent users are not one of those inputs.
whyWrong.b: Token count is a property of the text, not of the document's structure. A corpus of long, consistently structured policy PDFs is chunked along that structure, and 'appropriate' is doing real work in this objective.

explanation.analogy: Cutting a shelf into sections by where the brackets fall, not by a fixed length that happens to fit the wall.
explanation.takeaway: Chunking is driven by the source documents and the questions asked of them, not by the window size.
explanation.deepDive: The guide gives no chunk sizes, overlap values, or index types. What the objective supplies is the criterion - appropriateness - and the two things it is judged against.

source.section: 3.5 Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies

questions.reviewNote: Objective 3.5 names chunking and indexing but states no chunk sizes, overlap rules, or index types. The correct option is a defensible reading of 'appropriate', not a guide-specified rule. Confirm against fuller source material before treating the phrasing as exam-aligned.

questions.prompt: According to objective 3.6, what two things must a retrieval strategy be matched to?

options.text: The Claude model selected, and the context window it offers
The shape of the data, and the pattern of the query
The chunk size used, and how the pieces are indexed

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the objective names exactly two things to match against. Each distractor substitutes a pair of settings from a neighbouring decision, which is the only meaningful error here.

distractorRationale.a: Probes matching retrieval to the model rather than to the material and the question, conflating pipeline and model design.
distractorRationale.c: Probes substituting build-time settings for the query-time question - chunk size and indexing are the two decisions 3.5 names, not what 3.6 matches retrieval to.

explanation.correct: The objective's phrase is 'matched to data shape and query pattern'. Retrieval is chosen against two things: what the corpus looks like, and what the incoming queries look like.

whyWrong.a: The model and its window bound what can be sent, but they are not what retrieval strategy is matched to. That substitution moves the decision to 2.1.
whyWrong.c: Chunk size and indexing are pipeline-construction settings from 3.5. The pairing this objective states is about the material and the question, not about how the store was built.

explanation.analogy: A search strategy is chosen for what is in the collection and how people ask for things, not for how the building is wired.
explanation.takeaway: 3.6 matches retrieval to two inputs only: the shape of the data and the pattern of the query.
explanation.deepDive: The pairing is the objective's whole content: two inputs, and a strategy chosen to match them. Neither input is a setting you configure on the system — one describes the material being searched and one describes the request that arrives.

source.section: 3.6 Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern

questions.prompt: Which integration mechanisms does objective 3.7 ask an architect to choose between?

options.text: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC
Cached responses, reusable templates, and shared prompts
MCP, API/CLI, and agent-to-agent

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: a list of wire protocols, a prompt-reuse list from another domain, and the objective's own list. Objective 3.7 names exactly three mechanisms, so there is no basis for a fourth.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing transport protocols with the integration mechanisms the objective names.
distractorRationale.b: Probes carrying over a prompt-reuse list from another domain, which contains no integration mechanism at all.

explanation.correct: The bullet reads 'Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)'. Those three are the mechanisms being weighed.

whyWrong.a: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC are wire-level API styles. The objective names its three mechanisms explicitly in parentheses, and none of these is one of them.
whyWrong.b: Cached responses, reusable templates, and shared prompts are prompt reuse strategies from another domain. None of them is a way of connecting Claude to another system.

explanation.analogy: The protocol is the road; the integration mechanism is the kind of vehicle you chose to travel on it.
explanation.takeaway: 3.7 names three mechanisms: MCP, API/CLI, and agent-to-agent.
explanation.deepDive: Note the objective's own phrasing: 'evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism'. Evaluating the protocols and selecting the mechanism are one objective rather than two separate steps, and both halves belong to the same judgement.

source.section: 3.7 Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)

questions.prompt: Which pair of context strategies does objective 3.8 ask you to weigh?

options.text: Few-shot and zero-shot prompting
Progressive discovery and monolithic context
Semantic indexing and keyword indexing

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the objective's own pair, plus two pairs drawn from elsewhere in the guide that a candidate might reach for when thinking about context. Three is enough to test the pairing itself.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reaching for Domain 2's prompting vocabulary when the question is about how context is supplied.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for Domain 3's retrieval vocabulary, which describes how stored material is found rather than how much context arrives.

explanation.correct: 3.8 is 'Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy'. The two strategies it asks you to weigh are named directly in the bullet.

whyWrong.a: Few-shot versus zero-shot is 2.3's distinction, about examples inside a prompt. It does not describe how much context the system loads.
whyWrong.c: Semantic and keyword indexing are choices about the store 3.5 builds, not about how much context arrives. Supplying context is what 3.8 asks you to weigh.

explanation.analogy: Monolithic context is handing someone the whole manual up front; progressive discovery is handing them the index and fetching a chapter when they ask.
explanation.takeaway: 3.8 is about how much context arrives up front versus on demand: progressive discovery versus monolithic context.
explanation.deepDive: This is the only place in the guide where progressive discovery appears. Because the surrounding objectives all sound context-related, misattribution is the main risk, and the words 'progressive' and 'monolithic' are the anchors to hold on to.

source.section: 3.8 Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy

questions.prompt: Which set does objective 4.1 name as the evaluation metrics for a Claude-based system?

options.text: Accuracy, latency, and cost only, because safety and security are out of scope
Latency and cost only, because accuracy belongs to the model, not the system
Safety and security only, because accuracy and cost are optimization targets
Accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security, which is the full set the objective names

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, because objective 4.1's five-item list supports three genuinely different wrong metric sets: a quality-and-spend subset, a performance-and-cost subset, and a safety-only subset. Each probes a different way of trimming the list, not padding.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that safety and security live in a separate evaluation track rather than in the metric set itself.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusion between model-level and system-level measurement, and treats accuracy as someone else's metric.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the overlap between objective 4.1 (define the metric) and objective 4.5 (optimise cost and latency); cost and latency are metrics here.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.1 names five metrics in one list: accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security. All five belong to the set.

whyWrong.a: The objective lists all five measures together; it does not place safety and security out of scope for evaluation.
whyWrong.b: Accuracy is the first metric objective 4.1 names, and dropping it leaves a set that cannot measure output quality.
whyWrong.d: Dropping accuracy, latency, and cost leaves two of the five named measures. Cost and latency are metrics in 4.1 even though optimising them is 4.5.

explanation.analogy: A metric set is the checklist you agree on before you start measuring. Leave two items off and two whole classes of failure go unobserved.
explanation.takeaway: Evaluation metrics in this domain are accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security - all five, not a subset.
explanation.deepDive: Cost and latency appear in two different objectives: 4.1, where you define them as metrics, and 4.5, where you optimise them. Recognising that split is the main thing objective 4.1 is testing.

source.section: 4.1 Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)

questions.prompt: Which pair of deliverables does objective 4.2 ask an architect to produce?

options.text: A fixed set of scoring rules applied to each production response
A dashboard of production latency, token spend, and error rates
Evaluation datasets and test frameworks built using mixed methodologies
Two prompt variants run against live traffic until one outperforms the other

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options. The objective names exactly two artefacts (datasets, test frameworks) plus the mixed-methodology qualifier, and the three distractors are each a different job in the domain - a production rule set that belongs to no objective here, 4.6 monitoring, and 4.3 A/B testing. A fifth would repeat one of those mappings.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that an evaluation is a rule set attached to production, rather than a designed dataset plus a framework.
distractorRationale.c: Points at objective 4.6; monitoring live traffic is not evaluation design.
distractorRationale.d: Points at objective 4.3; comparing two variants is A/B testing, not building the test framework.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.2 names two artefacts - evaluation datasets and test frameworks - and adds that they should use mixed methodologies.

whyWrong.a: The objective names datasets and frameworks to be designed. It does not describe a rule set applied to each live response.
whyWrong.c: Latency, spend, and error-rate charts from live traffic are 4.6, monitoring with logging and observability tools.
whyWrong.d: Running two variants until one wins is 4.3, A/B testing and iterative improvement.

explanation.takeaway: 4.2 delivers two things: the evaluation datasets and the test frameworks that run on them.
explanation.deepDive: Note the wording order - datasets first, then frameworks. The datasets are the material; the framework is the harness that applies a mixed set of methodologies to it.

source.section: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies

questions.prompt: Objective 4.2 covers evaluation datasets and test frameworks. Which of these belongs to objective 4.5 rather than to 4.2?

options.text: Composing the test set and the framework that runs it
Trading token usage and latency against their cost
Choosing the mix of methodologies the test framework applies
Running an A/B test and iterating on whichever variant underperformed

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options so the item tests attribution rather than recall: two options are genuine 4.2 work and the keyed answer is 4.5, while the A/B option sits in 4.3 and is wrong on its own terms. Naming 4.5 in the stem leaves exactly one destination to match against, so a shorter list would make the odd one out obvious.

distractorRationale.a: Tests whether the reader knows dataset and framework construction is the core of 4.2 rather than something adjacent to it.
distractorRationale.b: Tests whether 'mixed methodologies' is read as part of framework design, which is how the objective words it.
distractorRationale.d: Tests the 4.2 versus 4.3 boundary: comparing variants and iterating on them is 4.3, so this option is wrong here, but not because it is 4.5.

explanation.correct: Trading token usage, latency, and cost against each other is objective 4.5, which optimises cost-performance trade-offs.

whyWrong.a: Composing the test set and the framework that runs it is precisely what 4.2 asks you to design.
whyWrong.b: Choosing the mixed methodologies is part of designing the test framework under 4.2.
whyWrong.d: Running an A/B test and iterating on the underperforming variant is 4.3. That is outside 4.2 too, but the question asks for 4.5, and 4.3 is not 4.5.

explanation.takeaway: 4.2 builds the datasets and the framework; 4.5 optimises the token, latency, and cost trade-off.
explanation.deepDive: This distinction matters in practice: an evaluation framework can report cost and latency as measurements (4.1) without 4.5's work of changing the system to improve them.

source.section: 4.2 Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies

questions.prompt: Which activity is objective 4.3?

options.text: Choosing which metrics will judge the system before any test is built
Cutting token usage to bring down the cost of each request
Comparing two variants and iterating on what the comparison reveals
Recording each production call so failures can be traced later

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, each a neighbouring objective in the same domain. The distinction is coarse (compare-and-improve versus define, optimise, or monitor), but each distractor sits on a different verb, so none is filler; a three-option version would have had to merge measure and monitor into one.

distractorRationale.a: Probes placing metric selection inside the A/B testing objective rather than with 4.1.
distractorRationale.c: Probes treating any improvement effort as iteration rather than as the cost optimisation that 4.5 owns.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating any improvement-driven activity as A/B testing rather than as 4.6 monitoring.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.3 is 'Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements' - comparing variants and then improving based on the result.

whyWrong.a: Choosing the metrics before any test exists is objective 4.1, define evaluation metrics.
whyWrong.c: Reducing token usage to lower per-request cost is objective 4.5, optimise cost-performance trade-offs.
whyWrong.d: Recording production calls for later tracing is objective 4.6, monitoring with logging and observability tools.

explanation.takeaway: 4.3 is the compare-and-improve loop: A/B testing combined with iteration on what the comparison shows.
explanation.deepDive: The objective names two things at once - a testing method and an improvement discipline - so a variant comparison that stops at 'A won' does not satisfy the whole objective.

source.section: 4.3 Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements

questions.prompt: Objective 4.4 names three things an architect should diagnose. Which set is it?

options.text: Prompt failure, hallucinations, and model mismatch
Latency spikes, token overruns, and cost regressions
Risks, limitations, and failure modes of the system
Bias, fairness, and transparency concerns

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because all three distractors are real triads from elsewhere in the exam, so the item tests whether the reader can place the correct triad under 4.4 rather than recognising a familiar list of three.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that performance and cost regressions are what 4.4 asks you to diagnose; they belong to 4.5 and 4.1.
distractorRationale.b: Probes cross-domain confusion - that triad is objective 5.2, not the 4.4 diagnostic list.
distractorRationale.d: Probes cross-domain confusion again - bias, fairness, and transparency is Domain 5 objective 5.5.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.4 is 'Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)'. All three named items are system issues.

whyWrong.a: Latency and cost are named as metrics in 4.1 and optimisation targets in 4.5. Objective 4.4 does not list them among the things to diagnose.
whyWrong.b: Risks, limitations, and failure modes is the wording of Domain 5 objective 5.2, a different objective in a different domain.
whyWrong.d: Bias, fairness, and transparency is Domain 5 objective 5.5, not part of the Domain 4 diagnostic triad.

explanation.takeaway: 4.4's diagnostic triad is prompt failure, hallucinations, and model mismatch.
explanation.analogy: Two of the three are things the system asserts wrongly (prompt, hallucination); the third is a mismatch between the system and the model running it.

questions.prompt: A prompt works on one Claude model and degrades when the team swaps models, with nothing else changed. Which category does objective 4.4 point to?

options.text: Prompt failure, the category objective 4.4 names for a system whose prompt stopped working
Model mismatch, the category objective 4.4 names for a system running an unsuited model
Hallucination, the category objective 4.4 names for a system that invents content
Cost regression, the category objective 4.1 tracks when spend per request rises

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options so all three of 4.4's categories appear plus one metric-side distractor. The scenario isolates a single category, so the item tests discrimination inside the triad rather than recall of the triad.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that a behaviour change with no prompt change is still a prompt failure.
distractorRationale.c: Probes attributing every degradation to fabricated output, without anything in the scenario indicating invented content.
distractorRationale.d: Probes reaching for the cost metric in 4.1 when the described symptom is quality, not spend.

explanation.correct: Only the model changed and quality changed with it. Objective 4.4 names model mismatch as one of the three things to diagnose, and this is exactly its case.

whyWrong.a: The prompt did not change. Objective 4.4 lists prompt failure as a separate category from model mismatch.
whyWrong.c: Nothing in the scenario describes invented or unsupported output. Hallucination is a named category but it is not what happened here.
whyWrong.d: Cost is an evaluation metric under 4.1 and an optimisation lever under 4.5. It is not one of the three things 4.4 asks you to diagnose.

explanation.takeaway: A behaviour change caused purely by a model swap is model mismatch - one of 4.4's three named categories.
explanation.deepDive: The three categories in 4.4 point at different layers: prompt failure is the instruction, hallucination is the output, and model mismatch is the pairing of system and model.

questions.reviewNote: Objective 4.4 names model mismatch as a diagnostic category but never defines it, so the keyed option depends on the standard sense of the term - a system paired with an unsuited model - and on the reading that a behaviour change with no prompt change is that category. The scenario matches the term rather than any guide-specified rule. Confirm against fuller guide text before treating the option wording as exam-aligned.

questions.prompt: A support assistant confidently quotes a discount policy the team never published. Neither the prompt nor the model has changed. Which of objective 4.4's three categories does this fall under?

options.text: Prompt failure, where the prompt stops producing the behaviour it was written for
Hallucination, where the system asserts content it has no basis for
Model mismatch, where the model running the system is unsuited to the task

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one per category objective 4.4 names. The scenario fits exactly one of them, so the item tests discrimination inside the triad rather than recall of a procedure, and a fourth option would have to be a category the objective does not name.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reaching for the prompt-layer category when the prompt is unchanged and the fault is in what the system asserted.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for the system-to-model pairing when the model has not changed and nothing about the task stopped fitting it.

explanation.correct: The prompt and the model are both unchanged, and the system has invented a policy that does not exist. Objective 4.4 names hallucination as one of the three things to diagnose, and this is its case.

whyWrong.a: Prompt failure is the other named category: the prompt stopped producing the behaviour it was written for. Here the prompt is untouched, so the fault is in what the system asserted rather than in what it was told.
whyWrong.c: Model mismatch is the pairing of a system with an unsuited model. Nothing changed about the model, and the task it is serving is the one it was already serving.

explanation.analogy: The clerk was told exactly what to do and still quoted a policy that does not exist. The instruction was not the problem; what came out was.
explanation.takeaway: The symptom points at the output layer: what the system asserted, not what it was told and not which model ran it.
explanation.deepDive: The three categories in 4.4 sit at different layers: the instruction, the output, and the pairing of system with model. Naming the layer a symptom appears at is the diagnostic move here, because each category sends you to a different place to look.

questions.prompt: Latency is fine but cost per request keeps climbing. Which objective covers the fix an architect chooses?

options.text: 4.1, which defines accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security
4.4, which diagnoses prompt failure, hallucinations, and model mismatch
4.5, which optimizes token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
4.6, which monitors system performance using logging and observability tools

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, one per relevant objective, each quoting that objective's own wording. The distractor that shares two of 4.5's keywords (4.1 also names cost and latency) is the one worth testing.

distractorRationale.a: The strongest distractor: 4.1 also names cost and latency, but as metrics you define rather than levers you optimise.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for diagnosis because rising cost 'feels like' a fault, rather than an optimisation target.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating a rising metric as a monitoring task - 4.6 observes, it does not improve.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.5 is 'Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs'. Choosing a change to bring cost down while holding latency is that work.

whyWrong.a: Objective 4.1 names cost and latency as metrics you define. The scenario asks for a fix, which is optimisation, not measurement.
whyWrong.c: Objective 4.4 covers prompt failure, hallucinations, and model mismatch. Rising cost is not one of those three.
whyWrong.d: Objective 4.6 observes a running system. Charting the climb would be monitoring; choosing the fix is 4.5.

explanation.takeaway: Measuring cost and latency is 4.1; changing the system to improve them is 4.5.
explanation.deepDive: The trade-off wording matters: 4.5 does not ask you to optimise each lever in isolation, and it does not oblige you to give something up. In this scenario token usage is the lever in play - sending fewer tokens per request is what improves cost-performance, with latency left where it already was. Read 4.5 as cost-performance gained by changing what the system sends.

questions.prompt: Which two means does objective 4.6 name for watching a running system?

options.text: Evaluation datasets and test frameworks
A/B tests and iterative improvements
Accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security
Logging and observability tools

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, because each distractor is a literal two-or-more-item phrase lifted from another objective in the domain. Testing the pair against the other lists keeps the item grounded without inventing tooling the source never names.

distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing offline evaluation design (4.2) with runtime visibility (4.6).
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing improvement work (4.3) with the observation capability that reports on it.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing what you measure (4.1) with the means you use to watch the system.

explanation.correct: Objective 4.6 is 'Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools'. Logging and observability tools are the two means it names.

whyWrong.b: Evaluation datasets and test frameworks are objective 4.2. They support offline evaluation rather than watching a running system.
whyWrong.c: A/B tests and iterative improvements are objective 4.3. That is how you change the system, not how you observe it.
whyWrong.d: Accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security are the metrics named in 4.1 - the quantities, not the means of monitoring.

explanation.takeaway: 4.6 names logging and observability tools as the means of monitoring system performance.
explanation.deepDive: The objective names categories of tool, not specific products. No platform is listed anywhere in the domain, so study the two categories rather than memorising a tool list.

questions.prompt: Which task belongs to objective 5.1?

options.text: Implement guardrails and safety controls
Identify the risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options, covering 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, and 5.5: the 5.1 verb plus the 5.2, 5.3, and 5.5 verbs verbatim. Compliance (5.4) is the one objective deliberately left out, because 'ensure compliance' sits close enough to guardrails and safety controls that a reader could defend either answer. Every remaining distractor is a real neighbouring objective, so the item tests verb-to-objective mapping rather than word recognition.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing building controls with the risk identification that precedes them (5.2).
distractorRationale.b: Probes placing human review inside guardrails rather than in its own objective (5.3).
distractorRationale.d: Probes folding ethics into safety controls rather than treating them as a separate objective (5.5).

explanation.correct: Objective 5.1 is 'Implement guardrails and safety controls'. The verb is implement - the work is putting controls in place.

whyWrong.a: Identifying risks, limitations, and failure modes is objective 5.2. That is analysis, not implementation.
whyWrong.b: Human-in-the-loop validation strategies are objective 5.3, a separate objective from guardrails.
whyWrong.d: Bias, fairness, and transparency are objective 5.5's ethical AI considerations, not the guardrail implementation of 5.1.

explanation.takeaway: 5.1 is the implementation objective: guardrails and safety controls go in.
explanation.deepDive: Every Domain 5 objective is a verb paired with an object, and that pairing is the reliable way to sort them. For 5.1 the verb is implement and the object is guardrails and safety controls, so the deliverable lives inside the system rather than in an analysis of it.
