questions.prompt: The team knows the system can be abused but has no control in place. Which objective covers the missing work?

options.text: 5.2, because risks and failure modes have not been implemented
5.1, because guardrails and safety controls have not been implemented
5.1, because the risks and failure modes have not been identified first
5.2, because guardrails and safety controls fall under ethics instead

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the 5.1/5.2 pair is the hardest boundary in this domain, so all four combinations of the two objective numbers and the two rationales are worth testing. A shorter list could not separate right-number/wrong-reason from wrong-number/wrong-reason.

distractorRationale.a: Right reasoning, wrong objective - it names the right gap but assigns it to 5.2.
distractorRationale.c: Right objective, wrong reasoning - it claims identification is missing when the prompt states the risks are already known.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong objective and a second misconception - it sends guardrails to 5.5 ethical AI.

explanation.correct: The risks are already identified in the scenario, so the missing work is building the controls. Objective 5.1 implements guardrails and safety controls.

whyWrong.a: Objective 5.2 is about identifying risks, limitations, and failure modes. You cannot implement a risk; the scenario's gap is a missing control.
whyWrong.c: The objective number is right but the reasoning is not - the prompt states the risks are known, so identification under 5.2 is not the missing step.
whyWrong.d: Guardrails and safety controls belong to 5.1, not to 5.5 ethical AI considerations, and they are not part of 5.2.

explanation.takeaway: 5.2 finds the risks; 5.1 builds the controls that answer them.
explanation.deepDive: As a rule of thumb for this domain: if the deliverable is a control in the system, it is 5.1. If the deliverable is a list of ways the system can go wrong, it is 5.2.

questions.prompt: Two items are open: putting controls in place inside the system, and showing the system meets a regulator's requirements. Which assignment is correct?

options.text: The controls are 5.4's work and the regulator demonstration is 5.1's work
Both are 5.1's work, because guardrails are how compliance is achieved
The controls are 5.1's work and the regulator demonstration is 5.4's work
Both are 5.4's work, because guardrails only matter where a regulation applies

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the correct split, the outright swap, and the two ways of collapsing the pair into a single objective. The two collapse options each earn a slot because they encode a real belief — that installing controls delivers compliance, or that controls are pointless without a regulation — and the swap catches a reader who has memorised the numbers without the work.

distractorRationale.a: Probes swapping the two objectives, the error a reader makes from memorising the numbers rather than the work they name.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the belief that compliance is produced by installing guardrails, which makes 5.4 look redundant.
distractorRationale.d: Probes the belief that guardrails only matter where a regulation applies, which makes 5.1 a special case of 5.4.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.1 covers controls that live inside the system. Objective 5.4 covers an obligation that sits outside the system, which the solution then has to be shown to meet.

whyWrong.a: This reverses the two. Building controls in the system is 5.1; demonstrating that the system meets a named regulation is 5.4.
whyWrong.c: The two objectives name different objects. Guardrails bound what the system does; GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP sit outside it, and installing controls does not by itself demonstrate that any of them is met.
whyWrong.d: 5.1 is not conditional on a regulation existing. The controls are the system's own safety behaviour, and they apply whether or not a named regulation is in scope.

explanation.takeaway: 5.1 builds controls inside the system; 5.4 demonstrates the system against an external regulation.
explanation.deepDive: Verb and object travel together in this domain, and that pairing is the reliable way to sort the objectives. Whenever two objectives look interchangeable, ask whether the object they name lives inside the system or outside it.

questions.prompt: Objective 5.2 asks an architect to identify three things. Which set is it?

options.text: Guardrails, safety controls, and escalation paths
Datasets, frameworks, and evaluation methodologies
Risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
Bias, fairness, and transparency concerns

The fourth slot earns its place because the cross-domain import is the error this item most needs to catch - an architect can recite the five 5.x objectives perfectly and still reach for evaluation terms here.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing the controls that address risks with the risks themselves - the 5.1 versus 5.2 boundary.
distractorRationale.c: Probes cross-domain import of Domain 4's evaluation vocabulary into a governance objective.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusion with 5.5, where bias, fairness, and transparency are ethical concerns rather than the risk-identification triad.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.2 is 'Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems'. The three objects of the verb identify are risks, limitations, and failure modes.

whyWrong.a: Guardrails and safety controls are objective 5.1. Controls are the response to risks, not the risks themselves.
whyWrong.c: Datasets, frameworks, and methodologies belong to objective 4.2 and have nothing to do with this governance triad.
whyWrong.d: Bias, fairness, and transparency are objective 5.5's ethical AI considerations, a distinct objective from risk identification.

explanation.takeaway: 5.2's three nouns are risks, limitations, and failure modes - and the verb is identify, not implement.
explanation.deepDive: The word 'identify' is what separates 5.2 from 5.1. An architect can satisfy 5.2 entirely in a risk register and still have done nothing for 5.1.

questions.prompt: Which objective covers placing people in the validation loop?

options.text: 5.1 Implement guardrails and safety controls
5.3 Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
5.2 Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
5.5 Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the correct 5.3 wording plus three other Domain 5 objectives whose wording could attract a 'human involvement' answer - guardrails (5.1), risk identification (5.2), and ethics (5.5). Each distractor is a real neighbouring objective with its own human element in practice, so no slot is filler.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that humans in the loop is a form of safety control rather than a validation strategy.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing who performs the validation with what analysts are asked to identify beforehand.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating fairness and transparency work as something that necessarily routes through human review.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.3 is 'Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies'. The phrase 'human-in-the-loop' is the defining wording of that objective.

whyWrong.a: Guardrails and safety controls are objective 5.1. A human reviewer in a validation path is not the same as a control in the system.
whyWrong.b: Identifying risks, limitations, and failure modes is 5.2 - analysis of the system, not a validation arrangement with people in it.
whyWrong.d: Bias, fairness, and transparency is objective 5.5. Those concerns can require human judgement without making 5.3 the right mapping for human-in-the-loop validation.

explanation.takeaway: Humans in the validation loop is 5.3 - the only objective in Domain 5 whose wording names human-in-the-loop explicitly.
explanation.deepDive: 5.1 and 5.3 are the pair most often swapped. The distinction in one line: 5.1 changes what the system is allowed to do; 5.3 puts a person in the loop for validation.

questions.prompt: Which three regulations does objective 5.4 name as its examples?

options.text: GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP
GDPR, PCI DSS, and SOC 2
HIPAA, SOX, and ISO 27001
FedRAMP, CCPA, and NIST AI RMF

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because each distractor is a set of real regulations in the same problem space, and every distractor shares at least one member with the correct set. That partial overlap is the point of the item - it stops the reader from matching on familiarity alone.

distractorRationale.a: Probes substituting PCI DSS and SOC 2 for two of the three that the objective actually names.
distractorRationale.b: Probes substituting SOX and ISO 27001 for GDPR and FedRAMP.
distractorRationale.d: Probes keeping only FedRAMP and filling the other two slots with adjacent privacy and AI frameworks.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.4 reads 'Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)'. All three named examples are GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP.

whyWrong.a: PCI DSS and SOC 2 are not named in the objective, even though GDPR is. Half right is still wrong for a named-example question.
whyWrong.b: HIPAA is named, but SOX and ISO 27001 are not. The objective's list is GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP.
whyWrong.d: FedRAMP is named, but CCPA and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework are not part of the objective's example list.

explanation.takeaway: The three regulations objective 5.4 names are GDPR, HIPAA, and FedRAMP.
explanation.deepDive: The objective marks these with 'e.g.', so they are examples rather than an exhaustive list. That matters: a distractor naming other real regulations is not automatically wrong in practice, but it is not what the objective states.

questions.prompt: The team has guardrails and a bias audit but cannot show it meets a regulator's requirements. Which objective is the gap?

options.text: 5.1, because guardrails and safety controls must extend to regulators
5.4, because the objective is compliance with regulations such as GDPR
5.5, because ethical AI work must be reported directly to the regulator
5.2, because risks and limitations must be logged for the regulator

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options because the scenario already satisfies 5.1 and 5.5, so the item tests whether the reader can rule those out from the facts and land on 5.4 rather than assume more of the same work is needed.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that strong controls automatically satisfy a regulator, which is exactly the assumption the scenario denies.
distractorRationale.c: Probes assuming that an ethics programme substitutes for a compliance position; 5.5 is not a reporting obligation.
distractorRationale.d: Probes treating the deliverable as a risk register when the scenario's gap is an external obligation.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.4 is 'Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)'. Being unable to show a regulator's requirements are met is precisely a compliance gap.

whyWrong.a: The team already has guardrails, so 5.1 is not the gap. Controls in the system do not by themselves establish compliance with a named regulation.
whyWrong.c: The bias audit is 5.5 work and is already done. Objective 5.5 addresses bias, fairness, and transparency - it is not a regulator reporting obligation.
whyWrong.d: Objective 5.2 identifies risks, limitations, and failure modes. The scenario's problem is an unmet external requirement, which is 5.4.

explanation.takeaway: Controls and audits are internal work; demonstrating compliance with a named regulation is 5.4.
explanation.deepDive: Controls and audits are internal work that shapes the system itself; the compliance obligation sits outside it. That inside-versus-outside test is what separates the two activities in this scenario.

questions.prompt: Which three concerns does objective 5.5 name under ethical AI?

options.text: Bias, fairness, and transparency
Latency, cost, and accuracy
Guardrails, escalation, and audit
Risks, limitations, and failure modes

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the correct 5.5 triad, the two neighbouring triads a reader is most likely to substitute (5.1's controls and 5.2's risk list), and one cross-domain import of evaluation-metric vocabulary. The fourth slot earns its place because that import is the error this item most needs to catch - an architect who knows all five 5.x objectives can still answer with measurement words instead of ethical ones.

distractorRationale.a: Probes cross-domain import of Domain 4's metric vocabulary into an ethics objective.
distractorRationale.b: A half-right guardrail triad - controls are real 5.1 work, but escalation and audit are not named anywhere in 5.5.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing 5.5's ethical concerns with 5.2's risks, limitations, and failure modes.

explanation.correct: Objective 5.5 is 'Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)'. Those three nouns are the whole of the objective's stated content.

whyWrong.a: Latency, cost, and accuracy are evaluation metrics from objective 4.1, not ethical AI considerations.
whyWrong.b: Guardrails belong to 5.1, and neither escalation nor audit is named in objective 5.5.
whyWrong.d: Risks, limitations, and failure modes are objective 5.2's list. They describe what can go wrong; 5.5 is about bias, fairness, and transparency.

explanation.takeaway: 5.5's ethical AI concerns are exactly three: bias, fairness, and transparency.
explanation.deepDive: All three nouns sit in one parenthetical, and the objective's verb is address — the ethical AI work is named here as a set of concerns, in the same shape as the three items objective 5.2 asks you to identify.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for "a chatbot that knows our documentation." Nothing has established what success means or what data is available. What should happen next?

options.text: Run structured discovery and requirement gathering with the stakeholders.
Document the target architecture so implementation can start.
Pick the model with the largest context window and begin prototyping.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one correct next step plus the two realistic anti-patterns (designing before discovery, prototyping before discovery). A fourth option would be filler with no distinct misconception to probe.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that the architect's first deliverable is a design document; 6.1 puts requirement gathering ahead of it.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that a capability choice substitutes for discovery, which is a model trade-off decision, not a requirements activity.

explanation.correct: Objective 6.1 covers structured discovery and requirement gathering, which is the work of establishing what the solution must do before any architecture is chosen.

whyWrong.a: Documenting an architecture assumes the requirements are already known. 6.1 is the phase that produces that understanding, and documentation under 6.4 follows a design.
whyWrong.c: Choosing a model is a trade-off decision made during design, not a substitute for gathering requirements. Objective 6.1 covers the conversation that establishes what is needed, not the comparison of capabilities that follows it.

explanation.analogy: A design drawn before discovery is a blueprint with no survey behind it.
explanation.takeaway: In Domain 6, structured discovery and requirement gathering come before any architecture is documented or decided.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 6.1 names two activities in one line — structured discovery, and requirement gathering — and both come before any architecture is chosen or documented.

questions.prompt: An architect has chosen a fixed workflow over an agentic design. What does objective 6.2 ask them to communicate?

options.text: Present the chosen option along with the trade-offs that drove it
Present the decision as final so implementation is not delayed
Omit rejected options so the team sees one clear path forward

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the correct framing plus two realistic communication anti-patterns (declaring rather than explaining, and hiding the alternatives).

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that authority replaces explanation; the objective names trade-offs, which cannot be conveyed by a bare decision.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that hiding alternatives is clarity; without the trade-offs stakeholders cannot evaluate the decision.

explanation.correct: 6.2 is communicating architectural decisions and trade-offs, so the decision and the reasoning behind it are both part of the message.

whyWrong.b: A decision presented as final carries no trade-offs at all, which is only half of what 6.2 asks for.
whyWrong.c: Removing the rejected options removes the evidence of the trade-off. The objective requires trade-offs to be communicated, not edited out.

explanation.takeaway: In 6.2 the trade-offs travel with the decision; a decision without its trade-offs is only half communicated.
explanation.deepDive: Trade-offs are also named elsewhere: 4.1's accuracy, latency, and cost metrics, and 6.3's SLAs, give the architect concrete material to put in front of stakeholders.

questions.prompt: A support assistant is live. Support leads keep raising complaints the team had not anticipated, and the architect carries each one back into the design. Objective 6.3 names two activities. Which one is happening?

options.text: The feedback loop, where stakeholder reaction keeps circulating back into the work
A one-off sign-off meeting where stakeholders approve the finished design
Expectation alignment, which is settled once before the service level is agreed

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the feedback-loop reading plus the two misreadings the objective's own wording invites - treating 6.3 as a single approval event, and collapsing feedback and alignment into the same activity. A fourth would have to assert a stakeholder practice the objective never describes.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reading 6.3 as a one-time event; the objective names a loop, and a finished design cannot take sign-off on work still in progress.
distractorRationale.c: Probes collapsing the objective's two halves into one, so that ongoing stakeholder input is mistaken for a service-level conversation that already concluded.

explanation.correct: 6.3 names two distinct things: stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment. Complaints that keep arriving and get routed back into the design are the feedback loop - stakeholder reaction circulating back into the work rather than being handled once.

whyWrong.a: A single approval meeting closes a conversation. The objective names a loop, and the scenario shows stakeholder reaction arriving repeatedly rather than once.
whyWrong.c: Expectation alignment is agreeing what the service will actually promise. Ongoing input about what users are actually seeing is the other half of the objective.

explanation.takeaway: 6.3 is two halves: aligning expectations, and keeping a feedback loop open once the system is live.
explanation.deepDive: The two halves answer different questions. Expectation alignment asks what stakeholders assume the service will do; the feedback loop asks what they report once it is running. An item that only tests the first half leaves the word 'feedback' untested - and the word is doing real work, because it marks the activity as recurring rather than concluded.

The stakeholder's expectation with the service level the solution can actually meet
The new service level with whatever the previous system promised

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the correct reconciliation plus two ways of anchoring expectation on an irrelevant reference (a model capability, or legacy behaviour).

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that expectation alignment means scaling a promise up to the best available capability.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that continuity with a previous system is the standard, ignoring what this solution can deliver.

explanation.correct: Expectation alignment is two-sided: the stakeholder's expectation and the service level the delivered solution can genuinely meet, which is where SLAs come in.

whyWrong.b: Aligning an expectation to a model capability is not expectation alignment; the commitment has to be something the operating solution can keep.
whyWrong.c: Anchoring on the previous system's promise ignores the requirements discovered for this solution, which is the opposite of requirement-driven alignment.

explanation.takeaway: Alignment is a two-way reconciliation between stakeholder expectation and what the solution can actually deliver.
explanation.deepDive: Alignment is two-sided because a commitment only means something if the solution can keep it. The parenthetical "(including SLAs)" on 6.3 is what ties the reconciliation to something measurable - a service level states how well the system performs, and the expectation has to be reconciled against that rather than against the best case the stakeholder hopes for.

questions.prompt: A decision has been explained. A stakeholder now asks for a written commitment to a response-time target. Which objective covers this next step?

options.text: 6.2 — Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
6.4 — Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
6.3 — Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options drawn from the three adjacent Domain 6 objective titles, which is exactly the distinction the item tests; no fourth objective applies to a target commitment.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that all stakeholder interaction stays in 6.2 once a decision has been explained.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that writing something down for engineers is the same as aligning a stakeholder's expectation.

explanation.correct: 6.3 covers stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment, and it explicitly names SLAs, so a requested service-level commitment is squarely 6.3.

whyWrong.a: 6.2 is about the decision and its trade-offs. Once that is done, agreeing a service-level commitment is expectation alignment, not decision communication.
whyWrong.c: 6.4 is documenting the architecture and giving implementers guidance. A target agreed with a stakeholder is not implementation guidance.

explanation.takeaway: 6.2 explains the decision; 6.3 agrees what the service will actually promise, SLAs included.
explanation.deepDive: The parenthetical '(including SLAs)' on 6.3 is the only place in the guide where SLAs are attached to an objective, which makes it a reliable anchor for questions about expectation alignment.

questions.prompt: Which activity is named directly by objective 6.4?

options.text: Documenting the architecture and giving implementers guidance on it
Gathering requirements before any design work has started
Announcing the agreed SLAs to sponsors and support leads

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the literal 6.4 activity plus one activity each from 6.1 and 6.3, which is the scope boundary being tested.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that written outputs belong to discovery; requirement gathering precedes any architecture to document.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that announcing service levels is documentation of an architecture.

explanation.correct: 6.4 is documenting architectures and providing implementation guidance, which has two halves: the record of the design and the guidance that lets engineers act on it.

whyWrong.a: Requirement gathering is 6.1. There is no architecture to document until the design exists.
whyWrong.b: Announcing SLAs is expectation alignment under 6.3, and it communicates a service level rather than an architecture.

explanation.takeaway: 6.4 has two deliverables: the documented architecture and the implementation guidance that travels with it.
explanation.deepDive: The pairing matters. Documentation without guidance leaves implementers to infer decisions; guidance without documentation cannot be maintained as the design evolves.

questions.prompt: 6.2 and 6.4 are separate objectives. Which statement separates them correctly?

options.text: 6.2 is for executives and 6.4 is for engineers, so the two never overlap
6.2 happens once, and 6.4 is repeated only when the design changes
6.2 is the discussion of a decision; 6.4 is the record plus implementation guidance

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the verb-based distinction the objectives actually state, plus an audience split and a frequency claim that neither objective implies.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that the two objectives are separated by audience; both serve the same architectural communication effort.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that documentation is only reactive; 6.4 accompanies the design work rather than waiting for changes.

explanation.correct: The objectives are separated by verb: 6.2 communicates decisions and trade-offs, 6.4 documents the architecture and provides implementation guidance. One is the exchange, the other is the durable record plus what implementers need.

whyWrong.b: Neither objective names an audience. 6.2 communicates decisions and trade-offs and 6.4 documents the architecture and provides implementation guidance, so the same architectural work is served regardless of who happens to read it.
whyWrong.c: 6.4 is not tied to a change event. The objective describes documenting and guiding as architect work, and 6.5 separately covers the iteration phase.

explanation.takeaway: 6.2 communicates; 6.4 records and guides. Same decisions, different verbs.
explanation.deepDive: Watch for questions that swap these two verbs. The guide's own wording is the only reliable tiebreaker: communicate = 6.2, document = 6.4.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the lifecycle phases named in objective 6.5?

options.text: discovery → design → handoff → monitoring → iteration
design → discovery → monitoring → handoff → iteration
handoff → discovery → design → iteration → monitoring

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options using the identical five phase names in different orders; the only honest way to test recall of a named sequence is to permute it.

distractorRationale.a: Puts design before discovery, reversing the phase that must inform it.
distractorRationale.c: Starts at handoff and moves iteration before monitoring, scrambling the back half of the lifecycle.

explanation.correct: 6.5 names the phases in order: discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration.

whyWrong.a: Design before discovery inverts the front of the lifecycle; discovery is the phase that feeds design.
whyWrong.c: Handoff cannot come first, and iteration is the phase that follows monitoring rather than preceding it.

explanation.takeaway: Domain 6's lifecycle runs discovery → design → handoff → monitoring → iteration.
explanation.deepDive: The five names form an ordered sequence, and the order is the content of the objective: each phase hands something to the next, with monitoring and iteration closing the loop rather than ending the lifecycle.

questions.prompt: A shipped solution is under monitoring and the team is deciding what to change next. Which objective covers the architect's work?

options.text: 6.4 — Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
6.5 — Support lifecycle phases, including monitoring and iteration
6.1 — Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options using the neighbouring objective titles at comparable length; the item is a scope boundary, not a technique, so a third and fourth option would only repeat the same test.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that ongoing work on a live system is primarily documentation work.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that any return to stakeholders means restarting discovery from the beginning.

explanation.correct: 6.5 supports the lifecycle phases, and monitoring and iteration are two of the five named phases, so work on a running system falls under 6.5.

whyWrong.b: 6.4 documents and guides implementation. Keeping a live system healthy is not documentation, even though decisions made there may be documented later.
whyWrong.c: 6.1 is the discovery and requirement activity that starts the lifecycle. Work inside the monitoring and iteration phases is not a return to discovery.

explanation.takeaway: Post-launch work on a live system is 6.5: it sits in the monitoring and iteration phases, not in 6.1 or 6.4.
explanation.deepDive: Monitoring and iteration are the two phases that sit after handoff, and together they describe work on a solution that is already running — which is what separates this scenario from anything in the earlier phases.

questions.prompt: Which activity is 7.1 rather than 7.2?

Tracing a production incident back to its root cause
Setting up the Claude tools and environments the team works in

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one activity per objective in Domain 7, which is exactly the boundary the item tests and needs no fourth.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the confusion between configuring the tooling (7.1) and improving the workflow with AI-assisted tooling (7.2).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between tooling setup and operational issue resolution, which is 7.3.

explanation.correct: 7.1 covers configuring the Claude tools and environments a team works in; the distinction being tested is the environment against the work the team does with it.

whyWrong.b: Changing how the team's process runs is the workflow improvement named in 7.2, not the tooling configuration named in 7.1.
whyWrong.c: Investigating and resolving a production issue is 7.3, operational issue resolution, and is unrelated to either configuration or workflow design.

explanation.takeaway: 7.1 configures the tools and environments; the objective that follows it changes how the work is done.
explanation.deepDive: The two objectives are separated by object, not by effort: 7.1 is about the environment, 7.2 is about the workflow.

7.3 — Support debugging and operational issue resolution

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that installing tooling completes the work of 7.1 and closes out the domain's enablement objectives.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that a team whose workflow is unchanged has an operational incident to resolve.

explanation.correct: 7.2 is improving developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling. Tooling in place without a changed workflow leaves the objective unmet.

whyWrong.a: 7.1 is configuration of the tools and environments, which the scenario says is already done; configuration does not stand in for workflow improvement.
whyWrong.c: 7.3 concerns debugging and operational issue resolution. No failure or incident is described, so this objective is not the open one.
